modules.title: Cut & Timing
modules.description: Master when and why to cut, cutting on action, eliminating dead air, and jump cuts.

lessons.title: Why Cut & Cutting on Thought
lessons.concept: Every cut must have a reason: to change perspective, advance the thought, or cut dead air. Never cut just because time passed.
lessons.why: Cutting before a thought completes confuses the viewer; cutting too late drains momentum.
lessons.bad_example: Leaving 1.2s of silent blinking after a sentence ends.
lessons.good_example: Cutting 0.1s after the speaker finishes their final syllable to bridge into the reaction or next line.

quiz.question: When should you make a cut during dialogue to maintain momentum?
options: Wait 2 seconds after the speaker stops talking
Right as the thought/syllable completes cleanly without lingering dead air
Always in the exact middle of every word
Only when the speaker blinks
quiz.explanation: Cutting right as the thought completes preserves meaning while maintaining conversational momentum.

modules.title: Pacing & Rhythm
modules.description: Understand shot duration, fast vs slow pacing, cadence, energy, and attention resets.

lessons.title: Shot Duration & Dead Air (Pacing 01)
lessons.concept: Pacing is the heartbeat of your video. In modern short-form and high-retention content, shots longer than 3–4 seconds without visual change cause viewer fatigue.
lessons.why: Human attention requires visual or auditory resets every 2.5–4 seconds. Leaving a static talking head for 5+ seconds makes the edit feel slow and uncurated.
lessons.bad_example: A static talking head lingering for 6.5s while repeating filler words or hesitating.
lessons.good_example: Trimming filler pauses, holding shots for 1.8–2.5s on average, and punctuating key moments with B-roll or punch-cuts.

quiz.question: What happens if a talking head shot runs for 6 seconds without any cut, zoom, or B-roll?
options: Viewer attention drifts and pacing feels sluggish
It automatically makes the speaker look smarter
The audio bitrate drops
Nothing, 6 seconds is standard for fast-paced shorts
quiz.explanation: Visual monotony causes attention drop-off. Fast modern edits introduce a cut, punch zoom, or B-roll every 2–4 seconds.

lessons.title: Rhythm & Changing Pace
lessons.concept: Pacing isn't just cutting fast all the time; it's about contrast. Fast sections create excitement; slower beats let key points land.
lessons.why: Monotonous speed (even fast speed) becomes numb without rhythmic breathing room.
lessons.bad_example: Every single cut is exactly 1.0 second from start to finish like a metronome.
lessons.good_example: Quick sequence of 1.2s cuts building tension, followed by a 3.0s breath before the climax.

quiz.question: Why is varying shot duration better than making every cut exactly 1.0 second?
options: It saves hard drive space
It creates musical rhythm and prevents visual numbness
DaVinci Resolve requires uneven cuts
It allows higher frame rates
quiz.explanation: Dynamic variety keeps viewers engaged by creating rhythm and emotional contrast.

modules.title: Story & Sequence
modules.description: Setup, conflict, progression, payoff, shot ordering, and information hierarchy.

lessons.title: Information Hierarchy & Setup
lessons.concept: Every edit tells a story. Order your shots so the viewer always understands what is happening before diving into details.
lessons.why: Showing the solution before the problem kills curiosity.
lessons.bad_example: Starting with random footage before explaining the premise.
lessons.good_example: Immediate context setup in 0-3s, followed by clear progression.

quiz.question: What is the primary role of the first 3 seconds in sequence storytelling?
options: Display copyright notices
Establish context and spark curiosity (Setup)
Play loud dubstep music
Fade in from black slowly
quiz.explanation: The setup establishes the stakes and hooks the viewer into caring about what follows.

modules.title: B-roll
modules.description: Why use B-roll, cover jump cuts, explain ideas visually, and create attention resets.

lessons.title: Show Instead of Tell
lessons.concept: Whenever the speaker describes an action, object, or feeling, show B-roll to reinforce the words visually.
lessons.why: Visuals complement auditory memory and keep the viewer visually stimulated.
lessons.bad_example: Speaker talks about editing software while only showing their face for 10 seconds.
lessons.good_example: Cut to screen recording of the timeline precisely as the speaker mentions the tool.

quiz.question: When should B-roll appear over talking head dialogue?
options: Only at the end credits
Right as the speaker introduces the concept to illustrate it and reset visual attention
Never, talking heads should never be covered
Whenever the audio is muted
quiz.explanation: B-roll shows what is being told and resets viewer attention.

modules.title: Audio & Transitions
modules.description: Dialogue leveling, SFX, music ducking, silence, J-Cuts, and L-Cuts.

lessons.title: The Power of the J-Cut
lessons.concept: A J-Cut occurs when the audio of the next scene starts before the visual cut occurs.
lessons.why: J-Cuts feel natural to human ears because in real life, we often hear something before we turn our eyes to look at it.
lessons.bad_example: Hard audio and video cuts happening simultaneously on every single shot.
lessons.good_example: Audio begins 0.4s ahead of the incoming B-roll clip.

quiz.question: What defines a J-Cut in video editing?
options: Audio from the next clip starts before the video changes
Video changes before the audio starts
Cutting the video shaped like the letter J
Muting the left channel
quiz.explanation: In a J-Cut, audio leads the visual transition, making cuts feel smoother and more immersive.

modules.title: Text & Caption
modules.description: Caption timing, keyword emphasis, visual hierarchy, and readability.

lessons.title: Keyword Emphasis & Reading Speed
lessons.concept: Captions shouldn't just transcribe; they should guide the eye. Highlight 1–2 power words per sentence.
lessons.why: Wall-of-text captions overwhelm the brain; synchronized word chunks enhance comprehension.
lessons.bad_example: A 4-line paragraph appearing all at once for 1.5 seconds.
lessons.good_example: 1–3 words per line, timed exactly to the spoken syllables.

quiz.question: Why is highlighting key words in captions beneficial?
options: It increases file size
It directs visual attention to critical insights quickly
It replaces the need for video
It bypasses copyright filters
quiz.explanation: Keyword highlights guide the viewer's eye and reinforce the speaker's emphasis.

modules.title: Motion
modules.description: Punch zooms, scale keyframes, position shifts, and motion emphasis.

lessons.title: Punch Zoom for Emphasis
lessons.concept: A punch zoom (scaling from 100% to 115–120%) acts as an instant visual punch to underline a punchline or crucial statement.
lessons.why: It simulates a multi-camera setup with a single camera angle and breaks visual stillness.
lessons.bad_example: Zooming randomly every 2 seconds without correlation to speech importance.
lessons.good_example: Punching in right on the climax word or surprising realization.

quiz.question: What is the optimal use of a punch zoom in talking head videos?
options: Continuous zooming in and out non-stop
To visually underline a key insight, punchline, or emotional pivot
Only when the camera battery is low
To hide out-of-focus background details
quiz.explanation: Punch zooms serve to emphasize crucial words or emotional turns.

modules.title: Hook & Retention
modules.description: First 1–3 seconds, curiosity gaps, pattern interrupts, and open loops.

lessons.title: The First 3 Seconds
lessons.concept: The first 3 seconds determine whether a viewer stays or scrolls away. No logos, no slow intros, no greeting.
lessons.why: Viewers decide in under 2 seconds if a video is relevant to their interests.
lessons.bad_example: 'Hey guys, welcome back to my channel! Today we are going to talk about...'
lessons.good_example: 'This single edit cut my render times in half—here is why.' (Instant visual hook).

quiz.question: What should be eliminated from the first 2 seconds of a video?
options: The audio track
Generic greetings, channel intros, and dead air before speech starts
The video colors
The primary subject
quiz.explanation: Jump straight into the core promise or intrigue without throat-clearing introductions.

modules.title: Color & Visual Consistency
modules.description: Exposure, contrast, white balance, shot matching, and basic color looks.

lessons.title: Shot Matching & Exposure
lessons.concept: Before grading for style, balance shots so skin tones and luminance match across cuts.
lessons.why: Jarring brightness shifts between A-roll and B-roll distract viewers from the content.
lessons.bad_example: Cutting from a warm bright shot to an underexposed green-tinted shot.
lessons.good_example: Matched skin tones and consistent contrast levels throughout the sequence.

quiz.question: What is the first step in color correction before applying creative LUTs?
options: Maximum saturation
Normalizing exposure, white balance, and contrast matching across shots
Inverting colors
Adding film grain
quiz.explanation: Ensuring baseline consistency between clips is essential before applying stylistic grades.

modules.title: Complete Edit
modules.description: Synthesizing Hook, Dialogue, B-roll, Music, SFX, Captions, and Pacing into a finished 30-60s short.

lessons.title: The 60-Second Master Edit
lessons.concept: Bring all 9 skills together: sharp hook, tight pacing, crisp audio transitions, well-placed B-roll, and clean caption hierarchy.
lessons.why: A great video editor harmonizes every layer into a single effortless viewer experience.
lessons.bad_example: Great cuts but muddy audio and a weak hook that loses 80% of viewers in 2 seconds.
lessons.good_example: A cohesive 45s short with high energy, clean sound design, and clear narrative payoff.

quiz.question: What distinguishes an advanced edit from a beginner edit?
options: Using as many 3D transitions as possible
Seamless harmony between sound, visual pacing, story momentum, and intentional cut timing
Making the video as long as possible
Using 10 different fonts
quiz.explanation: Mastery is intentional synergy where every cut and sound serves the emotional story.
